preamble: Fourteen solutions are of a kind (and not further defined)

clue.text: Judge in speculation having suffered loss

indicators.note: one thing set in another sits inside it, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: a bet is a speculation, a wager on an outcome
a ref, short for referee, judges a match

explanation.surface: A judge who gambled and lost everything.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Judge' looks like a court official, but here it is the umpire of a game, shortened in the usual way.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone bereft has been deprived of something precious, typically a loved one or a possession.

clue.text: Polish money given to fly-by-night?

parts.note: to buff is to polish a surface until it shines
a tip is money given for service

explanation.surface: Paying off a shady character who might skip town with the cash.
explanation.walkthrough: A fly-by-night is usually an untrustworthy dodger; the question mark lets it mean, literally, something that flies by night.
explanation.definitionFit: The buff-tip is a British moth, and moths are the insects that fly after dark.

clue.text: Get a mark for honest endeavour

parts.note: surface padding
the letters run across the end of the first word and most of the second
surface padding

explanation.surface: A student earning a grade for trying hard and honestly.
explanation.walkthrough: The same clue serves 24 Across, which hides its river in 'Get a mark'; this one lies in 'for honest'. The preamble says the fourteen rivers carry no definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The Rhone is a major European river flowing from the Swiss Alps through France to the Mediterranean.

clue.text: German suggestion of high cholesterol diet?

parts.note: fried food suggests a fatty, cholesterol-raising meal
a rich diet is one heavy in fat and cream

explanation.surface: Someone hinting that German cooking is heavy and fatty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'German' is not a nationality adjective here but a German person, named by a typically German first name.
explanation.definitionFit: Friedrich is a classic German given name, as borne by Frederick the Great and Nietzsche.

clue.text: Judge is well and truly scuppered

indicators.note: a scuppered ship is sunk, and words sunk together lose the gap between them

parts.note: surface padding
the two words read straight through with the space removed
surface padding

explanation.surface: A judge whose case has collapsed completely.
explanation.walkthrough: The river is simply two clue words run together; the preamble says the rivers are not otherwise defined.
explanation.definitionFit: The Welland is an English river flowing through Northamptonshire and Lincolnshire into the Wash.

clue.text: Notice sailors at home entertained by clown

indicators.note: a guest entertained by a host is taken in, so one piece is held inside another

parts.note: a wag is a joker or clown
RN is the Royal Navy
someone at home is in

explanation.surface: Sailors on shore leave being amused by a clown.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Notice' reads as a verb in the surface, but the answer is the noun: notice given in advance.
explanation.definitionFit: A notice can be an advance warning, as in giving someone notice of an impending change.

clue.text: Hoi polloi relish such nonsense

parts.note: surface padding
the letters straddle the end of one word and the start of the next
surface padding

explanation.surface: The common people love rubbish like this.
explanation.walkthrough: The river runs across 'polloi relish'; as the preamble says, the rivers have no definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The Loire is the longest river in France, famed for the chateaux along its valley.

clue.text: Galaxy with capital gets backing of publicity

parts.note: and means together with
Rome is the capital of Italy

indicators.note: backing means moving backwards, so these letters run the other way

parts.note: an ad, an advertisement, is publicity

explanation.surface: A galaxy, imagined as a city, attracting advertising money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Backing' sounds like financial support, but it reverses AD to DA at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Andromeda is the nearest large spiral galaxy to the Milky Way, visible to the naked eye.

clue.text: Old bird, about half size, to figure in square dance

indicators.note: half of a word keeps only part of it, so the rest is dropped
about means around, so one piece surrounds another

parts.note: the dodo is an extinct bird
the first half of the word

explanation.surface: An old, half-sized bird taking part in a barn dance.
explanation.walkthrough: The extinct bird splits around the half-word, leaving the hyphenated dance call.
explanation.definitionFit: A do-si-do is a square-dance move in which partners pass round each other back to back.

clue.text: Arrival with a message from the emperor

parts.note: surface padding
the letters run from the end of the first word through the next into the third
surface padding

explanation.surface: A courier arriving bearing an imperial message.
explanation.walkthrough: 19 Down has the same clue: it takes its river from the start of 'with a message', this one from the end of 'with' onwards.
explanation.definitionFit: The Thames is the river flowing through London into the North Sea.

clue.text: Explorer, at a pinch, captivated by royal bird?

indicators.note: a captive is held, so one piece is held inside another

parts.note: a kingfisher is literally a royal fisher, so the bird left after 'royal' supplies the king is a fisher
to pinch is to steal, to rob

explanation.surface: An explorer, in an emergency, enchanted by a regal bird.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At a pinch' reads as an idiom for 'if need be', but only 'pinch' does work. The question mark flags the playful reading of a kingfisher as a royal fisher.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Martin Frobisher was an Elizabethan seafarer who searched for the Northwest Passage.

clue.text: Wind usually from the west here

indicators.note: reading from the west means left to right, and here points to the words in front of you

parts.note: the letters run from inside the first word into the second

explanation.surface: Prevailing westerly winds in some location.
explanation.walkthrough: 'From the west' sounds like weather talk but just confirms the letters read left to right.
explanation.definitionFit: The Indus is the great river of Pakistan, rising in Tibet and flowing to the Arabian Sea.

clue.text: Real ignoramus, but we educated him

parts.note: surface padding
the letters straddle the end of the first word, all of the second and the start of the third
surface padding

explanation.surface: A teacher grumbling that a pupil stayed ignorant despite schooling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Real' sounds like a judgement on the ignoramus, but it is only surface; the river runs across 'but we educated'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Tweed forms part of the border between Scotland and England, flowing into the North Sea at Berwick.

clue.text: No byway, they say, where City used to play

indicators.note: what people say is spoken, so the spelling is judged by ear

parts.note: a road that is not a byway is a main road

explanation.surface: Giving directions to an old football ground, off the beaten track.
explanation.walkthrough: City is Manchester City football club, which played at Maine Road until 2003.
explanation.definitionFit: Maine Road was Manchester City's home stadium for most of the twentieth century.

clue.text: Daddy's legs for Mary

parts.note: pop is a familiar word for father, with the 's split off
pins is slang for legs

explanation.surface: A father lending his legs to a girl called Mary.
explanation.walkthrough: The possessive 's of 'Daddy's' is absorbed: POP plus PINS gives the surname.
explanation.definitionFit: Mary Poppins is the magical nanny of P. L. Travers's books and the Disney film.

clue.text: Raise for supporting subject for debate

indicators.note: in a down entry, a piece supporting another holds it up from below, so it comes second

parts.note: pro means in favour of
a motion is the proposition debated

explanation.surface: Arguing for a pay rise as a debating topic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Raise' is a noun here, as in a pay rise or a step up the ladder.
explanation.definitionFit: A promotion is an advancement in rank or position, a lift up the career ladder.

clue.text: Pagan gestures disconcerting congregation

parts.note: the letters straddle the end of the first word and the start of the second
surface padding

explanation.surface: Heathen gestures unsettling churchgoers.
explanation.walkthrough: The holy river of Hinduism hides in 'Pagan gestures', an apt place for it.
explanation.definitionFit: The Ganges is the sacred river of India, flowing from the Himalayas to the Bay of Bengal.

clue.text: Clubbing not far off, I felt

parts.note: nigh means near
taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone recalling a night out at a club close by.
explanation.walkthrough: There is no word signalling the rearrangement of 'I felt'; the setter relies on the solver spotting it from the crossing letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Clubbing, going out to dance at nightclubs, is a central part of a town's evening entertainment.

clue.text: Novel hero, the romantic type of course

parts.note: surface padding
the letters run from the end of the first word, through the second, into the third
surface padding, though a river is a watercourse

explanation.surface: A fictional hero who is, naturally, the romantic kind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Of course' sounds like 'naturally', but a river is a watercourse, a sly nod to the theme.
explanation.definitionFit: The Rother is a river in south-east England, flowing through Sussex and Kent to Rye.

clue.text: Gordian knot for Jupiter Pluvius?

indicators.note: a knot is a tangle, so these letters are twisted into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Asking for a hopelessly tangled problem to be solved by a Roman deity.
explanation.walkthrough: A Gordian knot is an intractable problem that Alexander cut through; here the knot simply tangles the word.
explanation.definitionFit: Jupiter Pluvius is the title of Jupiter as the sender of rain, so he is a deity of showers.

clue.text: Rover to display satisfaction with bird

definitions.meaning: first meaning: what a contented dog called Rover does
second meaning: a small songbird with a long bobbing tail

explanation.walkthrough: Rover is a stock name for a pet dog, and a happy dog swishes its tail from side to side.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase describes a dog's pleased gesture, and the same letters name a slender bird that bobs its tail.

clue.text: Arrival with a message from the emperor

parts.note: surface padding
the letters run from the start of the phrase across two word breaks
surface padding

explanation.surface: A courier arriving bearing an imperial message.
explanation.walkthrough: 8 Down shares the clue and finds its river later in the same phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: The Witham is a river in Lincolnshire, flowing through Lincoln to the Wash at Boston.

clue.text: The Hydra was a bird (in start of leading article)

definitions.note: the answer is an adjective completing the sentence

indicators.note: one thing in another sits within it, so a piece is placed inside
the start of a word is its opening letter alone

parts.note: its opening letter
an is the indefinite article
the erne is the sea eagle

explanation.surface: A note on the Hydra's origins, as a newspaper editorial might begin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leading article' reads as a newspaper editorial, but the two words act separately. The erne, a sea eagle, is a crossword regular.
explanation.definitionFit: Hercules slew the many-headed Hydra at Lerna, a marshy spot near Argos, so it is called the Lernean Hydra.

clue.text: Tree creature in retreat

parts.note: the ash is a common tree
a ram is a male sheep, a creature

explanation.surface: An animal backing away up a tree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Retreat' looks like a verb about withdrawing, but it is a noun: a place of seclusion.
explanation.definitionFit: An ashram is a Hindu religious community or hermitage, a secluded place for spiritual withdrawal.

clue.text: Remaining few having suffered loss, thirty docked

indicators.note: a docked tail is cut short, so the final letter is removed
something that has suffered is battered out of shape, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
the word minus its last letter

explanation.surface: Survivors counted after heavy casualties, thirty men short.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Having suffered loss' reads as a single phrase meaning bereaved, but 'having suffered' acts on 'loss' together with the cut-down 'thirty'.
explanation.definitionFit: A shortlist is the small group of candidates still in contention after the rest have been eliminated.

clue.text: Property that is owner-occupied, not rented

parts.note: surface padding
the letters straddle the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: An estate agent describing a house lived in by its owner.
explanation.walkthrough: The river hides in 'not rented', across the word break.
explanation.definitionFit: The Trent is a major river of the English Midlands, flowing through Nottingham to the Humber.

clue.text: Get a mark for honest endeavour

parts.note: the letters run from the end of the first word, through the second, into the third
surface padding

explanation.surface: A student earning a grade for trying hard and honestly.
explanation.walkthrough: 2 Down shares this clue and takes its river from 'for honest'; this one comes from 'Get a mark'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Tamar forms most of the border between Devon and Cornwall, reaching the sea at Plymouth.

clue.text: Some useful hints on property management

indicators.note: some of a phrase is only part of it, so the letters are taken from within

parts.note: the letters run from the end of the word before into the start of this one
surface padding

explanation.surface: A few handy tips for landlords.
explanation.walkthrough: The river starts in the end of 'Some' and runs into 'useful'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Meuse flows from France through Belgium and the Netherlands, where it is called the Maas.

clue.text: Suffering from catarrh in early life

parts.note: surface padding
the letters run from the end of the first word, through the second, into the third
surface padding

explanation.surface: Someone who had a runny nose as a child.
explanation.walkthrough: The river runs from the end of 'catarrh' into 'early'; there is a sly nose joke too, since rhin- means nose.
explanation.definitionFit: The Rhine flows from the Swiss Alps through Germany to the North Sea in the Netherlands.

clue.text: Arch emperor — not second in rank, thanks!

indicators.note: one thing in another sits within it, so a piece is placed inside

parts.note: a grade is a rank or level

indicators.note: not means without, so a letter is taken away

parts.note: the Arch of Titus stands in the Roman Forum, so he is the emperor known for an arch
S is the abbreviation for second, which is removed

explanation.surface: An exclamation thanking a lofty ruler for not ranking him second.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Arch' reads as an adjective meaning chief, but it points to the triumphal arch in Rome built for Titus.
explanation.definitionFit: Gratitude is the feeling of being thankful, so it stands in for thanks as a noun.

clue.text: Very small number put on record

parts.note: minute means tiny
D is the Roman numeral for 500

explanation.surface: A tiny figure entered into the books.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Very small' is the adjective minute, pronounced my-NEWT; 'number' is a Roman numeral.
explanation.definitionFit: To minute a meeting is to write up its formal record, so something minuted has been officially noted.

clue.text: Was this ever noticed by anybody affected?

parts.note: surface padding
the letters run from the end of the first word, through the second, into the third
surface padding

explanation.surface: A sceptic asking whether anyone really saw an effect.
explanation.walkthrough: The longest British river runs from the end of 'this' into 'noticed'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Severn is Britain's longest river, flowing from Wales through Shrewsbury and Gloucester to the Bristol Channel.
